items.title: Who rules Iran
items.sum: Iran is an Islamic republic in which an unelected Supreme Leader has the final say over the armed forces, the courts and state media. An elected president and parliament run the government within limits set by clerical councils. The Supreme Leader now is Mojtaba Khamenei.
items.detail:
Supreme Leader: The top post, held for life. Ruhollah Khomeini held it from 1979 to 1989 and Ali Khamenei from 1989; Mojtaba Khamenei, Ali's son, has held it since March 2026. The leader commands the armed forces and appoints the heads of the judiciary, the military and state broadcasting, and half of the Guardian Council.

Clerical councils: The Assembly of Experts, 88 clerics elected for eight years and chaired by Mohammad-Ali Movahedi Kermani, chooses the leader and can in theory remove him. The Guardian Council, six clerics named by the leader and six jurists approved by parliament and led by Ahmad Jannati, vets every candidate for elected office and can veto laws. The Expediency Council, chaired by Sadegh Amoli Larijani, settles disputes between parliament and the Guardian Council and advises the leader.

Elected bodies: The president is elected for four years and runs the government and the economy. Masoud Pezeshkian has held the post since July 2024; Abbas Araghchi is foreign minister. The 290-seat parliament (Majlis) is led by speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf.

Judiciary: The head of the judiciary is appointed by the leader. Gholam-Hossein Mohseni-Ejei has held the post since July 2021.

Security council: The Supreme National Security Council, chaired by the president, sets defence, security and nuclear policy, subject to the leader's approval. Its secretary since August 2026 is Mohsen Rezaei, a former commander of the Revolutionary Guards.

Armed forces: Iran has two militaries: the regular army (Artesh), commanded by Amir Hatami, and the Revolutionary Guards (IRGC), commanded by Ahmad Vahidi. The General Staff above both is led by Ali Abdollahi. The Basij militia, part of the IRGC, is led by Hossein Taeb.

The Timeline: For how these posts changed hands in the war, see Lion's Roar and Epic Fury.

items.title: The Revolutionary Guards and the Quds Force
items.sum: The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) was set up in 1979 to protect the revolution and has become Iran's most powerful institution, with its own ground, naval and missile forces, a militia and a large business empire. Its Quds Force runs Iran's operations and allies abroad.
items.detail:
Origins: Khomeini founded the Guards by decree on 5 May 1979 as a force loyal to the revolution, alongside the Shah's former army. They answer to the Supreme Leader, not the president. They grew up in the war with Iraq, and many of today's commanders are veterans of it.

Structure: The IRGC has ground, naval and aerospace forces, the last of which controls most of Iran's missiles and drones, plus the Basij militia and the Quds Force. Estimates of its strength range from about 125,000 to 190,000. Its navy patrols the Gulf and the Strait of Hormuz with fast attack boats.

The Basij: A volunteer militia of students, workers and villagers, founded in 1979. In war it supplies manpower; at home it guards the streets and helps put down protests.

The economy: Through its engineering arm Khatam al-Anbiya and linked firms and foundations, the IRGC holds large stakes in oil and gas, construction, ports, telecoms and trade, and profits from moving goods around sanctions. Former commanders hold many senior political posts.

Quds Force: The external branch trains, arms and funds allied groups abroad. Qasem Soleimani led it from about 1998 and built Iran's network in Iraq, Syria, Lebanon and Yemen. His deputy Esmail Qaani has led it since 2020.

Leaders now: The commander is Ahmad Vahidi, named on 1 March 2026, a former Quds Force chief and defence and interior minister. Argentina accuses him of a role in the 1994 AMIA bombing in Buenos Aires, which he denies.

Terror listings: Canada and several other states list the IRGC as a terrorist organisation. The US listing of 2019 is in the Timeline: Maximum pressure.

The Timeline: For the Guards' commanders killed and their wars since 2015, see Soleimani and the shadow war, and Lion's Roar and Epic Fury.

items.title: The 1953 coup and the 1979 revolution
items.sum: In 1953 a coup backed by the US and Britain toppled Prime Minister Mohammad Mosaddegh and strengthened the Shah. In 1979 a mass revolution ended the monarchy and Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini founded the Islamic Republic. Months later students seized the US embassy and held 52 Americans for 444 days.
items.detail:
1953: Mosaddegh nationalised the British-run oil industry in 1951. On 19 August 1953 he was overthrown in a coup organised by the CIA and Britain's MI6 with royalist officers, and Mohammad Reza Shah ruled with growing power. The CIA acknowledged its role in documents released in 2013.

The Shah: He pushed rapid modernisation and land reform from 1963 and ruled through the SAVAK secret police. Khomeini, a senior cleric who led opposition to him, was exiled in 1964.

Revolution: Protests and strikes grew through 1978. The Shah left Iran on 16 January 1979, Khomeini returned from exile on 1 February, and the monarchy fell on 11 February. After a referendum, the Islamic Republic was declared on 1 April 1979. A constitution approved in December 1979 placed a senior cleric, the Supreme Leader, above elected officials, under Khomeini's doctrine of guardianship of the jurist (velayat-e faqih).

Hostage crisis: On 4 November 1979 students loyal to Khomeini stormed the US embassy in Tehran and took its staff hostage. 52 Americans were held for 444 days. A US rescue mission failed in April 1980, and the US cut diplomatic relations, which have never been restored. The hostages were freed on 20 January 1981 under the Algiers Accords.

Consolidation: In the early 1980s the new rulers pushed out or crushed rival groups, from liberals to leftists and the MEK. Khomeini died on 3 June 1989, and the Assembly of Experts chose Ali Khamenei to succeed him.

items.title: The Iran–Iraq war
items.sum: Iraq under Saddam Hussein invaded Iran in September 1980. The war lasted almost eight years, killed hundreds of thousands and ended without a winner, and it still shapes how Iran's leaders think about defence.
items.detail:
The invasion: Iraq invaded on 22 September 1980, hoping to seize the oil province of Khuzestan while Iran was weakened by the revolution. Iran halted the advance, retook Khorramshahr in May 1982 and then carried the war into Iraq.

The long war: The fighting settled into trench warfare. Iran sent waves of young volunteers, many from the Basij, against Iraqi lines. Iraq used chemical weapons against Iranian troops and, at Halabja in March 1988, against Iraqi Kurds. Both sides fired missiles at each other's cities and attacked oil tankers in the Gulf.

The US: In the tanker war the US Navy escorted Kuwaiti tankers, and in April 1988 it destroyed Iranian oil platforms and warships. On 3 July 1988 the USS Vincennes shot down Iran Air Flight 655, killing all 290 people on board; the US said the crew mistook it for a warplane.

The end: On 18 July 1988 Iran accepted UN Security Council Resolution 598, and a ceasefire took effect on 20 August 1988. Khomeini compared the decision to drinking poison. Estimates of the dead range from several hundred thousand to about a million.

The legacy: Iran fought largely alone under an arms embargo, while Iraq had wide foreign backing. Its leaders drew three lessons: make your own weapons, above all missiles, after the war of the cities; fight enemies far from Iran's borders through allied forces; and rely on the IRGC, which grew up in the war. Many of today's commanders are veterans of it.

items.title: The shadow war with Israel: how it began
items.sum: Years before the open wars, Israel and Iran fought a covert war: a cyberattack on a nuclear plant, killings of scientists, sabotage, and Israeli strikes on arms bound for Hezbollah. Israel rarely confirmed its role, and Iran answered through its allies.
items.detail:
Stuxnet: A computer worm discovered in 2010 damaged about 1,000 centrifuges at Natanz in 2009–2010. It is widely reported to have been built by the US and Israel; neither has confirmed it.

Scientists: Four Iranian nuclear scientists were killed in Tehran between January 2010 and January 2012, several by bombs that motorcyclists stuck to their cars. Iran blamed Israel, which did not comment.

Iran's answer: In February 2012 bombs targeted Israeli diplomats in New Delhi and Tbilisi, and a plot in Bangkok fell apart when a bomb went off early. In July 2012 a bus of Israeli tourists was bombed at Burgas in Bulgaria, killing five Israelis and the driver; Bulgaria blamed Hezbollah.

Syria: From 2013 Israel struck convoys and stores of weapons bound for Hezbollah in Syria, and from 2014 it hit Iranian officers and Hezbollah commanders there.

How it works: Each side hits the other's people and plants without open war. Israel does not claim its strikes, and Iran works through the Quds Force and its allies, so both can deny.

The Timeline: What followed is in The nuclear deal and Soleimani and the shadow war.

items.title: The axis of resistance
items.sum: Iran built a network of allied armed groups across the region, which it calls the axis of resistance: Hezbollah in Lebanon, the Houthis in Yemen, militias in Iraq and Palestinian groups in Gaza. Assad's Syria was the land link that held it together until Assad fell.
items.detail:
Hezbollah: Founded in Lebanon in 1982 with the help of IRGC officers after Israel's invasion, it became Iran's strongest ally, with a large arsenal of rockets and missiles. It fought Israel in 2006. Its leader now is Naim Qassem.

The Houthis: The Ansar Allah movement from northern Yemen fought six wars with the Yemeni state from 2004, took the capital Sanaa in September 2014, and faced a Saudi-led coalition from March 2015. Iran supplies missile and drone technology.

Iraqi militias: Groups such as Kata'ib Hezbollah and Asa'ib Ahl al-Haq were built with Quds Force help to fight US forces after 2003. Many joined the state-funded Popular Mobilisation Forces, formed in 2014 to fight ISIS.

Palestinian groups: Iran has given money, weapons and training to Hamas and Palestinian Islamic Jihad in Gaza. Islamic Jihad is the closest to Iran; Hamas, a Sunni group, broke with Iran over Syria in 2012 and later mended ties.

Syria: Iran and Hezbollah helped keep Bashar al-Assad in power through the civil war that began in 2011, and Syria was the land route for Iranian arms to Lebanon. Since Assad's fall (see the Timeline: Gaza and the first direct blows), Syria's rulers have been hostile to Iran, so that route is cut.

How it works: The Quds Force supplies weapons, money, training and advisers, while each group keeps its own leaders and local aims. This lets Iran put pressure on its enemies from a distance while denying direct responsibility.

The Timeline: For the axis's wars since 2015, see Gaza and the first direct blows, and Lion's Roar and Epic Fury.

items.title: The nuclear programme
items.sum: Iran says its nuclear programme is peaceful, but it has enriched uranium to 60%, close to weapons grade, and the UN nuclear watchdog could not confirm it had no military aims. Its main plants are badly damaged, and inspectors have not checked its stockpile since June 2025.
items.detail:
The sites: Natanz is the main enrichment plant, with underground halls. Fordow is a smaller enrichment plant built inside a mountain near Qom. Isfahan holds uranium conversion plants and tunnels used for storage. Arak is a heavy-water reactor that could have made plutonium. Bushehr is a Russian-built power reactor, on the grid since 2011.

The early years: The programme began under the Shah with US help in 1957. In August 2002 an exiled opposition group revealed secret sites at Natanz and Arak, and in September 2009 the US, Britain and France exposed Fordow. US intelligence judged that Iran had run a weapons effort until 2003. From 2006 the UN Security Council imposed sanctions, and the US and EU added oil and banking sanctions in 2012. An interim deal in Geneva in November 2013 froze parts of the programme while talks went on.

Enrichment: Power reactors use uranium enriched to 3–5%; weapons use about 90%. Each step up takes less work, so 60% uranium is most of the way to weapons grade. By June 2025 the IAEA counted about 440.9 kg of 60% uranium, enough for about ten weapons if enriched further.

Breakout: Breakout time is how long it would take to make enough weapons-grade uranium for one bomb. Building a working warhead and a way to deliver it would take longer.

The IAEA: Iran joined the Non-Proliferation Treaty in 1970. The IAEA, the UN's nuclear watchdog, inspects its declared sites and reports to a board of 35 states, which can refer Iran to the UN Security Council.

Now: Fordow, Natanz and Isfahan are badly damaged. The IAEA estimated in March 2026 that just over 200 kg of 60% uranium remained in tunnels at Isfahan, with more at Natanz, but it has not been able to check.

The Timeline: The deal, the strikes on the sites and the inspectors' exit are in The nuclear deal, Talks and the twelve-day war, and Lion's Roar and Epic Fury.

items.title: Missiles and drones
items.sum: Iran has the largest and most varied missile force in the Middle East, built mostly at home after the war with Iraq, and it mass-produces cheap attack drones such as the Shahed. It supplies weapons and know-how to its allies, and drones to Russia.
items.detail:
Origins: In the war of the cities in the 1980s Iran had few missiles to answer Iraq's. It bought Scuds from Libya, Syria and North Korea, then learned to build its own; the Shahab-3, based on North Korea's Nodong, was first tested in 1998.

The arsenal: Before the 2025 and 2026 wars, US commanders put Iran's ballistic missiles at more than 3,000. Most belong to the IRGC Aerospace Force, and many are kept in underground bases that Iran calls missile cities.

Ranges: Short-range Fateh-family missiles reach about 300–700 km. Missiles that can reach Israel include the liquid-fuelled Shahab-3, Ghadr and Emad, with ranges of about 1,600–2,000 km, and the solid-fuel Sejjil and Kheibar Shekan. Iran says it limits its range to 2,000 km. It also has cruise and anti-ship missiles and a space launch programme.

Drones: The Shahed-136 is a cheap one-way attack drone with a range of well over 1,000 km, built to be launched in swarms. Larger drones such as the Mohajer-6 and Shahed-129 carry bombs and cameras.

Russia: Russia uses Shahed drones, which it calls Geran-2, against Ukraine and now builds them itself at Alabuga in Tatarstan.

The axis: Iran sends missiles, drones, parts and know-how to Hezbollah, the Houthis, Iraqi militias and Hamas, often for local assembly.

The Timeline: For Iran's missile and drone attacks, see Gaza and the first direct blows, Talks and the twelve-day war, and Lion's Roar and Epic Fury.

items.title: Oil, sanctions and the Strait of Hormuz
items.sum: Oil is Iran's main export, and most of it now goes to China, sold at a discount through a shadow fleet. Sanctions, war and mismanagement have sent the rial crashing and inflation soaring. The Strait of Hormuz, on Iran's southern coast, carried about a fifth of the world's oil before the war.
items.detail:
Reserves: Iran holds some of the world's largest oil and gas reserves, and shares the giant South Pars gas field with Qatar. Kharg Island handles most of its crude exports.

Sanctions before 2015: The US has had sanctions on Iran since 1979 and banned most trade in 1995. UN sanctions over the nuclear programme began in 2006. In 2012 the EU banned Iranian oil and Iranian banks were cut off from the SWIFT network; exports fell from about 2.5 million barrels a day to about 1 million.

China and the shadow fleet: In 2025 Chinese refiners bought about 1.38 million barrels a day of Iranian oil, over 80% of its exports, by Kpler's count, mostly small independent refineries known as teapots. The oil moves on ageing tankers that switch off their trackers and transfer cargo at sea, and it is often relabelled as coming from other countries. The US has sanctioned hundreds of these ships.

The rial: A dollar cost 70 rials in 1979 and about 135,000 on the open market in 2018. By late September 2026 it cost about 2.5–2.7 million. Inflation ran around 40% in 2025 and above 80% in 2026. Parliament has approved removing four zeros from the currency.

Hormuz: The strait links the Gulf to the Gulf of Oman and is about 33 km wide at its narrowest. In 2024 about 20 million barrels of oil a day passed through it, about a fifth of world consumption, plus about a fifth of world LNG trade, mostly from Qatar.

Why it matters: Only Saudi Arabia and the UAE have pipelines that bypass the strait, with about 2.6 million barrels a day of spare capacity. Iran lines its coast and islands, including Abu Musa and the Tunbs, which the UAE claims, with missiles, mines and IRGC fast boats.

The Timeline: For sanctions since 2015 and shipping in the current war, see Maximum pressure, Snapback and the road to war, and Lion's Roar and Epic Fury.

items.title: Protests and the opposition
items.sum: Iran has seen waves of mass protest, each put down by force, from the student riots of 1999 to the Green Movement of 2009. The opposition is split between monarchists, the MEK and Kurdish and Baluch armed groups.
items.detail:
1999: In July 1999 police and militiamen raided a Tehran University dormitory after a protest over the closing of a reformist paper, and days of riots followed.

2009: Millions protested after Mahmoud Ahmadinejad was declared the winner of the 12 June 2009 election over Mir Hossein Mousavi. The Green Movement was crushed within months, and Mousavi and Mehdi Karroubi have been under house arrest since 2011.

How protests are put down: The Basij and riot police clear the streets, the internet is cut, and thousands are arrested. Revolutionary Courts hand down long sentences and, in some cases, death sentences.

Monarchists and the MEK: Reza Pahlavi, the last Shah's son, lives in the US and calls for a secular, democratic transition. The MEK (People's Mojahedin), a leftist Islamist group that fought the Islamic Republic and sided with Iraq in the 1980s, is led by Maryam Rajavi and based in Albania. Thousands of its members and other prisoners were executed in 1988.

Ethnic groups: Kurdish parties such as the KDPI, Komala and PJAK keep bases in Iraqi Kurdistan, which Iran strikes with missiles and drones. In Sistan and Baluchestan the Sunni militant group Jaish al-Adl, founded in 2012, attacks security forces.

The Timeline: For the protests of 2022 and the crackdown of January 2026, see Soleimani and the shadow war, and Snapback and the road to war.
